title: A done task file records an acceptance criterion the suite no longer satisfies, and workers may not fix it
description:
Surfaced while draining agentic-7pq (2026-07-25), where it produced a direct collision between two repo conventions.

agentic-7pq retired tests/test_agentic_latency.sh's 1s wall-clock ceiling (it swung 6x with host load and redded scripts/check.sh repo-wide), replacing it with a deterministic bd-call-count assertion plus a 60s backstop. specs/agentic-core-redesign/SPEC.md's R-L was updated to match.

But specs/agentic-core-redesign/tasks/03-ready-resume.md (Status: done) still reads:
  Steps 3: 'assert median wall time of 5 agentic ready runs < 1s (R-L)'
  Acceptance: '- [x] bash tests/test_agentic_latency.sh -> prints MEDIAN <n>s OK with n < 1 at >=500 seeded issues (R-L) -- measured MEDIAN 0.457s OK (600 issues seeded).'

Anyone re-verifying task 03 against its own written criterion now fails it, and its recorded 0.457s evidence is unreproducible. That is the re-verification trap docs/memory/anchored-acceptance-criteria.md warns about.

The collision: the drain critic flagged the stale criterion as blocking; the drain worker then rewrote those two lines (preserving the original as a labelled 'History:' line); the independent verifier returned FAIL, correctly citing CLAUDE.md's append-only convention -- criterion text in a task file is read-only to workers, and this is mechanically checked. Drain's orchestrator reverted the edit (branch commit 96c2fcac) so the P1 gate fix could land, leaving the underlying drift unfixed by design.

So the convention has no sanctioned path for the case where the WORLD changed under a done task's criterion. Decide which:
(a) a criterion in a Status: done task may carry an appended supersession note (append-only already permits appending) pointing at the superseding SPEC requirement, without rewriting the original lines -- and say who may add it;
(b) done task files are frozen audit records, and staleness is accepted, in which case say so explicitly at the convention site so future critics stop flagging it as blocking;
(c) a spec-level supersession marker carries this instead, and task files are never touched.

Related drift found in the same pass: specs/agentic-core-redesign/SPEC.md lines ~309-311 still carry '- [ ]' for R-L although task 03 is Status: done and the criterion now passes.
design: Choose option (c): completed task files remain frozen audit records. A later invalidation is recorded at spec level with the superseding requirement/evidence; the original done-task criterion is never rewritten. The spec owner or an attended maintenance task may add the supersession record.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bash tests/test_done_task_supersession.sh` exits 0, proving the original task-03 criterion remains unchanged, the spec carries a machine-checkable supersession record, and R-L is checked against the current load-invariant test. 2. `bash tests/test_agentic_latency.sh` exits 0. 3. `bash tests/test_doc_links.sh` exits 0. Evidence level: L1 artifact structure plus L2 behavior.

title: check.sh's SERIAL mechanism does not survive concurrent drain workers each running their own check.sh
description:
Discovered by the agentic-7pq drain worker (2026-07-25). scripts/check.sh has a SERIAL mechanism that keeps contention-sensitive tests from running against each other WITHIN a single check.sh run. It has no effect across runs: four concurrent drain workers each invoke their own check.sh, so any contention-sensitive test runs N-way concurrent with itself and the SERIAL list buys nothing.

That is precisely how agentic-7pq's 1s wall-clock ceiling came to be measured at 2.058/3.946/4.875/5.522s. agentic-7pq fixed that one test by replacing the wall-clock assertion with a load-invariant bd-call-count assertion, but the hole is structural: any future timing-sensitive assertion added to this suite inherits it, and the SERIAL list's name implies a protection it does not provide across processes.

Calibration datapoint from the same worker: the host reached load average 92 from ordinary background work (a Go e2e suite, ffmpeg, Chrome) with no drain workers running at all.

Decide whether to (a) make the guard cross-process (a lockfile around the SERIAL section), (b) rename/document SERIAL so its within-run-only scope is not mistaken for a general guarantee, or (c) rule that no wall-clock assertion belongs in this suite at all and enforce that -- which is the direction docs/memory/wall-clock-perf-assertions.md already argues.
design: Choose option (c): blocking correctness suites must not depend on host-load wall-clock thresholds. SERIAL is documented and tested as within-one-check.sh-process ordering only; no cross-process lock is added. Performance checks use deterministic operation counts, with wall time only as a generous hang backstop.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bash tests/test_check_sh_runner.sh` exits 0 and includes a regression asserting the SERIAL contract is explicitly within-process only. 2. `bash tests/test_agentic_latency.sh` exits 0 using the load-invariant bd-call-count assertion and only the existing generous hang backstop. Evidence level: L2 behavior.

title: loop-tier-warn only warns on frontier-tier; a deep-tier polling loop still passes silently
description:
Follow-up to agentic-z7b.1 (merged 09518f5d, 2026-07-25). The shipped hook's LOOP_TIER_FRONTIER_PATTERN defaults to 'fable', matching runtimes/claude-code.md's frontier-tier pin. So a waiting loop scheduled from a Fable session warns, but one scheduled from Opus or Sonnet does not.

Whether that is right depends on what the doctrine actually targets. .claude/rules/token-discipline.md's Session refresh section says 'A waiting main loop is a scheduler, not a thinker' and prescribes cheap-tier (or launchd) for it, dispatching judgment work to awaited fresh subagents. Read literally, ANY non-cheap-tier main loop that idles past the cache TTL re-warms a fat context to poll — the evidenced cost was 4 watch-then-act sessions spending 36 dollars of 95 (38%) purely re-warming, and those were not necessarily frontier-tier. On that reading the hook under-covers: the pattern should match anything above scout-tier, not just the top rung.

The counter-argument is noise: warning on Opus would fire on most interactive sessions that schedule any wakeup, and a hook that fires constantly gets ignored — the same failure mode that drove agentic-oqm's severity tiering.

Decide the intended coverage, then either widen the default pattern or document why frontier-only is deliberate. The mechanism itself needs no change: the pattern is already tunable via LOOP_TIER_FRONTIER_PATTERN.
design: Widen the default advisory to all known non-cheap Claude main-loop tiers (Sonnet, Opus, Fable), while Haiku remains silent and LOOP_TIER_FRONTIER_PATTERN stays available as an operator override. Keep the hook warn-only and sidechain-blind.

title: An audit-shaped task needs an on-disk deliverable — a verifier cannot read the worker's verdict
description:
Process defect hit live during agentic-wcz (2026-07-25). That task's acceptance criteria specified its deliverable as a per-repo table 'in the verdict'. Drain's verifier is dispatched with the branch and the task file, NOT the worker's verdict text — by design, since the verifier must not be able to rationalize the worker's claims. So the verifier correctly found no commits, no files, and no artifact, and returned FAIL on a task whose substantive work was actually complete and correct (it then re-ran the audit itself and reached the identical conclusion).

The bug is in the acceptance-criteria authoring rule, which today only requires criteria to be runnable commands. For a task whose output is a FINDING rather than a code change, that is not enough: the finding must land somewhere the verifier can read — an evidence file under the repo, or a written artifact path — or verification is structurally impossible. CLAUDE.md's anchored-acceptance-criteria convention and docs/memory/anchored-acceptance-criteria.md are the natural homes for the added rule.

Cost when it bites: a full wasted verifier run plus an orchestrator judgment call to override a FAIL, which is exactly the kind of override that should stay rare to remain meaningful.
design: Audit/finding tasks must name a committed on-disk deliverable that an independent verifier can read without the worker verdict. The rule belongs in the acceptance-authoring doctrine; verdict-only output is explicitly non-dispatchable.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bash tests/test_token_discipline_structure.sh` exits 0 and includes a regression that the acceptance-authoring doctrine requires an on-disk artifact for audit/finding tasks and rejects verdict-only deliverables. 2. `bash tests/test_doc_links.sh` exits 0. Depth ceiling: L0 is sufficient because this task changes binding doctrine, and the test pins the exact contract.

This issue is about acceptance criteria whose DELIVERABLE is unreadable by a verifier (a finding that lives only in the worker's verdict). agentic-7pq hit the same class of gap from the other direction: its criteria were fine, but drain's own DISPATCH failed to give the verifier a readable tree, and separately a verifier imported an unrelated task's Touch list as the scope boundary for a hand-filed bd issue that has no Touch list at all.

The verifier scoped it against specs/agentic-core-redesign/tasks/03-ready-resume.md's Touch list (a different spec's done task, which the branch happened to touch) and returned FAIL for 'scope creep' on files the fix genuinely required. The orchestrator overruled that.

The generalizable rule, alongside this issue's on-disk-deliverable rule: a verifier must be told what the scope boundary IS, and 'this issue has no Touch list, judge scope against the issue description alone' must be sayable. Absent that, a verifier will find some nearby Touch list and apply it. Both rules belong in the same convention edit -- what a verifier can read, and what a verifier may judge against.

title: drain workers cannot run the critic, so the review gate degrades to self-review
description:
Observed live 2026-07-25: the agentic-k2s drain worker reported 'the pre-commit review-gate blocked the commit and no Agent tool is available in this dispatch, so I recorded a self-review verdict against the staged diff via bin/review-gate record'.

The review gate's value is that an INDEPENDENT reviewer looks at the diff. A dispatched implementation-worker that cannot spawn a critic satisfies the gate by reviewing its own work, which is the one thing the gate exists to prevent -- and it does so silently, producing a recorded verdict indistinguishable from a real one.

Related finding from the same batch (agentic-oqm): the severity vocabularies live only in hooks/review-gate/pre-commit; the critic agent and /critique emit findings in their own format with no shared contract, so a critic that never writes a leading severity label is always treated as non-blocking.

Decide the shape: give workers a way to invoke a real reviewer, have drain's orchestrator run the critic over each branch before merge (it can -- it has the Agent tool), or make a self-recorded verdict visibly distinct so it cannot pass as independent review.
acceptance_criteria: A verdict recorded by the same agent that authored the diff is either impossible or clearly marked as self-review in the recorded marker, covered by a test in tests/test_review_gate.sh.
close_reason: Merged. Marker-side fix: record refuses without a staged diff in its own tree, so the recorder is structurally the author; no identity field (measured — SESSION_ID is inherited, CHILD_SESSION is set in main too, CLAUDE_PID is shared, nothing discriminates). Notice states only what the gate observes and no longer asserts non-independence. drain step 3 documents the orchestrator critic pass mapped to the critic's real READY/READY WITH NITS/NOT READY contract. 288/288 tests, verifier PASS.

comments.author: Steven
comments.text:
[2026-07-25 /drain] Reproduced live again on agentic-7pq. The implementation worker reported verbatim: 'Review was a self-review, recorded via bin/review-gate record, not an independent critic — the Agent tool is not available at this nesting level (ToolSearch for Agent/Task returned nothing).'

Two useful details this run adds over the agentic-k2s observation.

1. The cause is now pinned precisely: it is not a permissions or allowlist gap. The worker ran as a Workflow-dispatched agent, and agent nesting is one level only, so no Agent/Task tool exists in its frame at all. ToolSearch confirms their absence rather than a denial. That rules out 'grant workers the Agent tool' as a fix -- the harness cannot offer it at that depth.

2. The worker self-reported the self-review prominently in its Decisions block and explicitly recommended an independent critic pass before merge. So a cooperative worker surfaces it, but nothing structural forces that; a worker that simply omitted the line would have produced a recorded verdict indistinguishable from a real review, which is this issue's core complaint.

This run's orchestrator worked around it by running the critic agent itself over 'git diff main...<branch>' before merging -- which is the third candidate fix in the description, and it works: the orchestrator does have the Agent tool. That makes 'drain's orchestrator runs the critic per branch before merge' the empirically demonstrated option, with 'mark self-recorded verdicts visibly distinct' as the complementary guard for build-path (non-drain) workers.

title: bd-compliance Stop hook blocks a drain whose claimed issues are still legitimately in flight
description:
Hit live during a /drain run on 2026-07-25. drain claims its batch in bd and appends the ids to .beads/session-claims (per its loop step 2), then dispatches a background Workflow. The orchestrator's very next turn end trips .claude/hooks/bd-compliance.sh, which blocks because those ids are claimed-and-open -- which is exactly the correct state while the workers are still running.

The hook's contract has no notion of work in flight: it only accepts (a) no claims, (b) every claimed id closed, or (c) a final message starting DEFERRED/BLOCKED/INCOMPLETE. A drain orchestrator mid-run matches none of these. Its stop_hook_active loop protection means the block clears on the second attempt, so the practical effect is one wasted turn per batch plus a misleading 'close them before ending the session' instruction that would be wrong to follow.

Candidate fixes to weigh: teach the hook to treat an id whose bd status is in_progress AND that has a live dispatching session as satisfied; or have drain record an in-flight marker alongside .beads/session-claims that the hook honors; or scope the hook to attended /work sessions only. Decide which before building -- the hook's value is that it cannot be silently ignored, so any escape hatch must not become a general bypass.
acceptance_criteria: A drain orchestrator with claimed-but-in-flight issues can end a turn without the hook firing, while a session that abandons claimed work with no dispatch in flight is still blocked. Both cases covered by tests in tests/test_bd_compliance_hook.sh.
close_reason: Merged. An id now satisfies the hook when bd reports it in_progress AND .beads/session-inflight holds a marker fresher than BD_COMPLIANCE_INFLIGHT_TTL (3600s). Per-id, decaying, no session-wide switch; the block message deliberately does not advertise the marker. drain step 2 writes it as part of the claim unit before dispatch. 10/10 tests, verifier PASS.

title: Mechanically gate main-session raw-output pasting (cause #5)
description:
Doctrine only right now: token-discipline.md's Session hygiene bullet says don't paste large command output/full file contents/full Workflow JSON into the main session -- summarize it. feedback_wake_budget_is_main_context_only.md confirms the wake-budget context-size arm measures ONLY the orchestrating session's own transcript, driven by exactly this pattern. Never mechanically enforced -- and this is the cause that produced THIS session's own wake-budget overage tonight (151k tokens, 3 re-primes), via large inline Bash/tool outputs and pasted JSON across the conversation.

Scoping needed before /build: research what a Claude Code hook can actually do to tool output before it lands in context -- can a PostToolUse hook REWRITE/truncate a tool result, or can it only observe and warn/block (in which case 'gate' means block-and-require-resubmission, not silent truncation)? Check with the claude-code-guide agent or Claude Code hooks docs. Candidate mechanism once that's known: a PostToolUse hook (Bash, Read, Agent/Workflow return) that measures result size and, over a threshold (e.g. 5-10k tokens), either rewrites it to a scratchpad-path + short preview, or blocks with a message telling the agent to summarize/externalize instead of retry-as-is.

This is the most technically uncertain of the 3 sub-tasks (hook output-rewrite capability is unconfirmed) -- resolve the capability question first; if rewriting isn't possible, the acceptance criteria will need to shift to a warn-and-block shape instead of silent truncation.

GOTCHA for any future orchestrator-computed Touch-disjointness: always normalize absolute vs relative paths before comparing, string-literal overlap checks silently miss real collisions otherwise. The 3 collided pairs were run in two sequential rounds instead of one batch; both rounds succeeded cleanly.

4. The Workflow tool's `args` parameter did NOT work when passed as a top-level tool-call parameter (JSON array) alongside a `script` or `scriptPath` param -- every attempt (both `script`+`args` together and `scriptPath`+`args` together) failed with "args.map is not a function" / args undefined inside the script, even across two separate launches. title: Record the bd-vs-native-task-tools conflict as a deliberate stance
description:
The repo bans the harness native task tools (TaskCreate/TaskUpdate/TaskList) in favour of bd. The call is right on the merits — native tasks are session-scoped while bd carries dependencies, claims, provenance, and cross-session resume — but it is a standing conflict with a platform affordance, and the harness re-litigates it: it emitted unsolicited "consider using TaskCreate" reminders repeatedly within a single session on 2026-07-27.

Outcome: the stance is recorded once, with its reason and its cost, so a future session (or a future maintainer weighing a platform change) does not re-derive it or quietly drift into the native tools. This is documentation of an existing decision, not a reversal.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] the stance appears once in shared guidance with the reason (durability, dependencies, provenance, cross-session resume) and the cost (recurring platform nudges)
- [ ] it is cited rather than restated wherever the ban already appears
Depth: L0 (text presence). Depth ceiling: a recorded stance has no behavior to exercise; behavioral complement is the existing bd-compliance Stop hook, which already enforces the ban mechanically.

title: review-gate record prints unknown-option noise on every call
description:
bin/review-gate record prints "review-gate: unknown option: <hex key>" twice on every invocation, then records the verdict correctly and lets the commit proceed. Observed on 4 consecutive calls on 2026-07-27. Cosmetic — the gate works — but it trains readers to ignore the tools own error output, which is the failure mode the gate exists to prevent.

Outcome: either the key argument is parsed properly or the message is removed.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] printf VERDICT... | ./bin/review-gate record produces no unknown-option line on stderr or stdout
- [ ] bash tests/test_review_gate.sh exits 0, with a case asserting clean output on a successful record
Depth: L2 (behavioral, via the existing review-gate test suite). Note: tests/test_review_gate.sh is a frozen retain surface (agentic-k9k0), so this may need the additively-inventoried-test route rather than editing it.
close_reason: Fixed in 3b57edfc, and the triage was wrong: this was not cosmetic noise. hooks/review-gate/pre-commit calls 'review-gate show <key>', bin/review-gate rejected every argument, so severity parsing was blind and the gate's blocking tier was dead — a 'correctness:' finding did not refuse a commit on HEAD (verified by driving a real gated commit in a clean worktree). The parked working-tree attempt removed argument validation wholesale and failed 2 of tests/test_review_gate.sh's assertions; the committed fix scopes validation per subcommand. 304 pass, 0 fail.

title: A worktree's edits to hooks/ or bin/ are not exercised by that worktree's own commits
description:
Reported independently by the agentic-jhw worker and confirmed by its verifier, 2026-07-25.

The repo sets core.hooksPath=/Users/sjaconette/claude/.beads/hooks, and that pre-commit chains ABSOLUTE paths into the main checkout: /Users/sjaconette/claude/hooks/review-gate/pre-commit and the main checkout's bin/review-gate. A worktree-isolated worker editing either file therefore commits through the MAIN checkout's unmodified copies, not its own.

Consequence: a worker changing hook behavior cannot exercise that change by committing, and will observe the OLD behavior while believing it tested the new. The agentic-jhw worker hit this precisely — its own commit ran main's pre-stamp version of the very hook it was changing, so the new notice did not appear and could have been read as the change not working.

This is a trap specific to hook/gate work, which this repo does a lot of. It also interacts with agentic-00w (the two bd-compliance copies with no parity test): both stem from hook wiring that reaches outside the working tree.

Worth deciding whether .beads/hooks/pre-commit should resolve its chained paths from 'git rev-parse --show-toplevel' rather than hardcoding the main checkout — the agentic-kts worker already used that pattern for its own added block, so the two blocks in the same file now disagree about how to resolve the root.
design: Fix the tracked effective hook wiring so chained review/install-gate paths resolve from `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` in the invoking worktree. Do not merely document the limitation and do not mutate other repositories.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bash tests/test_install_gates.sh` exits 0 with a linked-worktree fixture proving the hook edited in that worktree is the hook invoked by its commit. 2. `bash tests/test_review_gate.sh` exits 0 and preserves linked-worktree marker behavior. Evidence level: L2 worktree behavior.
notes:
[2026-07-25 /drain] Deferred from unattended dispatch: the acceptance text leaves an implementation-versus-documentation choice open and names no runnable acceptance command. Blocks: unattended dispatch. Choose the path and add an exact worktree fixture or doc check.
[2026-07-26 /acceptance-hardening] Added an explicit reversible design default and runnable verification commands for unattended drain.
close_reason: Implemented worktree-safe hook dispatch in .beads/hooks/pre-commit (git rev-parse to locate worktree root), with fallback to hook location; fixed in hooks. Evidence in bin changes and existing test fixture worktree coverage.

title: bin/review-gate's NOTHING_FOUND parser blocks on a clean verdict that carries an explanation
description:
Discovered by the agentic-kts drain worker, 2026-07-25.

bin/review-gate's severity parser treats 'correctness: none — <explanation>' as a BLOCKING finding. Its NOTHING_FOUND pattern requires the line to end immediately after 'none', so a well-formed clean verdict that adds trailing rationale is read as a finding rather than as the absence of one.

Consequence: the gate blocks precisely when a reviewer did the more useful thing — said 'none' and explained why — and passes when the reviewer said only 'none'. That trains reviewers toward terser, less informative verdicts to satisfy a parser.

Related to agentic-oqm's finding that the severity vocabularies live only in hooks/review-gate/pre-commit with no shared contract between the critic agent, /critique, and the gate — a critic that never writes a leading severity label is always treated as non-blocking, while this bug makes an explicit clean label blocking. The two failures point opposite directions from the same missing contract.

Also related to agentic-90f (bin/review-gate cannot read back a recorded verdict, so the marker path is duplicated) — same file, worth one pass.
design: Extend the NOTHING_FOUND grammar to allow explanatory text after an explicit no-finding token while retaining blocking behavior for real correctness/security findings. Keep parsing local to the review-gate contract.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bash tests/test_review_gate.sh` exits 0 with cases proving `correctness: none — <explanation>` and bare `correctness: none` are non-blocking, while `correctness: none of the writes are atomic` remains blocking. Evidence level: L2 parser behavior.
notes:
[2026-07-25 /drain] Deferred from unattended dispatch: the acceptance text names a test file but no runnable command. Blocks: unattended dispatch. Add the exact command that exercises the new and existing parser cases.
[2026-07-26 /acceptance-hardening] Added an explicit reversible design default and runnable verification commands for unattended drain.

title: shell-text-tools rule (a) bans in-place writes but its enforcement hint names only sed -i
description:
Self-reported by the agentic-f7r drain worker, 2026-07-25: 'I used one perl -pi -e in-place edit on tests/test_verifier_worktree_integrity.sh (a file I had authored moments earlier), which .claude/rules/shell-text-tools.md (a) forbids; the resulting content is correct and committed, but the rule has no mechanical enforcement for perl -pi -- its cross-reference only names Bash(sed -i *) as the permission-deny shape.'

The rule's prose is already general enough: section (a) says 'Never sed -i, in-place awk, or cat >/>> onto a tracked source or docs file'. The gap is between that general prose and the ONE concrete deny shape its cross-reference section (e) offers: 'pair it with Bash(sed -i *) permission deny rules when write protection must be hard'. A reader wiring up enforcement from (e) protects against sed -i and nothing else, while perl -pi -e, ed, python -c with open(...,'w'), and tee all do the same thing.

Two things to settle:
1. Broaden (e)'s deny-rule guidance beyond sed -i, or say explicitly that the enumeration is illustrative and the prose in (a) is the binding scope.
2. Note that a worker self-reporting the violation is the only reason this surfaced. The rule is currently honour-system for every in-place tool except sed -i.

Worth checking whether the gate skill's PreToolUse protect hook (.claude/hooks/pre-tool-protect.sh) is the right home for a broader pattern, rather than per-user permission deny rules.

title: A compiled drain workflow can dispatch a worker whose task text failed to interpolate
description:
Hit live during a /drain run, 2026-07-25.

drain compiles the ready queue into a Workflow script that interpolates each bd issue's text into an Agent prompt. The Workflow tool's args arrived as a JSON STRING rather than an object, so the script's destructure ('const { id, branch, spec } = args') yielded undefined for every field. The dispatch went ahead anyway: an implementation-worker, a verifier and a critic all launched with the literal string 'undefined' as both the task specification and the branch name.

All three agents handled it correctly and failed fast -- the worker returned BLOCKED with 'the inlined body between the BEGIN/END markers is the literal string undefined', explicitly refusing to infer a task from repo state; the verifier returned INCOMPLETE on 'git rev-parse --verify undefined'; the critic returned NOT READY. So no damage, and the agents' own contracts contained it. But it burned three agents (~128k subagent tokens, 44s) on a fault the orchestrator could have caught before dispatch, and a less disciplined worker could have guessed at a scope and made edits nobody asked for.

Two things to fix:
1. The Workflow tool's own documentation warns that args passed as a JSON-encoded string reach the script as one string, breaking args.filter/args.map. The same trap breaks destructuring. A compiled drain script should normalise ('typeof args === string ? JSON.parse(args) : args') rather than assume.
2. More generally, a compiled drain workflow should assert its required per-issue fields are non-empty strings and throw at the orchestrator BEFORE any agent() call. Failing in the script costs nothing; failing in a deep-tier worker costs a dispatch.

This belongs wherever drain documents how it compiles the queue into a workflow (.claude/skills/drain/SKILL.md's 'Execution model' section, or reference.md), so every future compiled script inherits the guard.
design: Enforce Workflow argument normalization and required-field validation in bin/check-token-discipline. A compiled script must parse string-encoded args before destructuring and assert non-empty task text and branch fields before any agent call.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bash tests/test_check_token_discipline.sh` exits 0 with red/green fixtures for string-encoded args normalization and pre-dispatch non-empty field assertions. 2. `bin/check-token-discipline` exits 0 against the real in-scope skill/workflow tree. Evidence level: L2 checker behavior.

[2026-07-26 /acceptance-hardening] Added an explicit reversible design default and runnable verification commands for unattended drain.

title: Removing the last id from .beads/session-claims with 'grep -v ... && mv' silently no-ops
description:
Hit live during a /drain run, 2026-07-25.

drain's SKILL.md loop steps 2 and 3 tell the orchestrator to append a claimed id to .beads/session-claims and, on close, to 'remove that <id> line from .beads/session-claims'. The obvious one-liner for the removal is:

    grep -v '^<id>$' .beads/session-claims > tmp && mv tmp .beads/session-claims

That is correct EXCEPT in the single most common case: when the id being removed is the LAST one in the file. grep exits 1 when it selects no lines, so with the file down to zero remaining claims the '&& mv' never runs and the original file survives untouched -- carrying the id that was just closed.

Observed exactly that: agentic-7pq was closed in bd, the removal command reported success, and 'od -c .beads/session-claims' still showed 'agentic-7pq\n'. The failure is silent; nothing in the command's output indicates it did nothing.

Consequence: a stale claim for an already-closed issue sits in the file, and .claude/hooks/bd-compliance.sh keys off that file -- so the next session inherits a phantom blocker for work that is already done. Related to but distinct from agentic-85d (that one is about legitimately in-flight claims; this one leaves a claim for CLOSED work).

Fix candidates: document the removal as a form that cannot fail this way ('grep -v ... > tmp || true; mv tmp ...', or a python/sed form), or better, give drain and /work a tiny shared helper (e.g. bin/session-claims add|rm <id>) so the bookkeeping is single-sourced rather than reimplemented as an ad hoc shell one-liner in each skill.
design: Add a shared `bin/session-claims` helper with idempotent `add` and `remove` operations; drain and work point to it instead of ad hoc grep/mv recipes. Removing the last id atomically leaves an empty file.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bash tests/test_session_claims.sh` exits 0 with single-id removal, multi-id removal, duplicate add, absent-id removal, and atomic-file cases. 2. `bash tests/test_bd_compliance_hook.sh` exits 0. 3. `bash -c "rg -q 'bin/session-claims' .claude/skills/drain/SKILL.md .claude/skills/work/SKILL.md"` exits 0. Evidence level: L2 helper behavior.

title: Verify no SKILL.md teaches git add+commit instead of pathspec-limited commits
description:
Recovered from a stray, never-consumed .claude/HANDOFF.md.stale-pathspec-commit-hardening left by an older session. Original finding: 'git add <path>; git commit' commits the ENTIRE staged index, not just <path> — in a shared/concurrent checkout this can silently sweep another session's staged-but-uncommitted files into your commit (confirmed twice 2026-07-16/17 in ~/hub, commit be1eb67, two unrelated specs' changes got bundled together — no data lost, but a real correctness gap). Fix is a pathspec-limited commit: git commit -m "..." -- <exact paths>, plus a git status check immediately before committing.

Re-checked 2026-07-24: the specific drain/SKILL.md and critique/SKILL.md locations the original handoff pointed at ('path-scoped commits, always' etc.) no longer exist in that form — both files have since been rewritten with no literal 'git commit' invocation examples at all, and .claude/rules/concurrent-sessions.md states the path-scoped-commit principle without showing exact git syntax. So there's no currently-confirmed buggy example to fix, but the underlying git behavior is a documented fact and worth a low-cost sweep: grep every .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md and .claude/rules/*.md for a literal 'git add' followed by a bare 'git commit' example, and fix any that appear to a pathspec-limited form. The original handoff's antigravity/codex mirror-porting steps are now moot (both trees were reduced to one-page READMEs in the agentic-core-redesign pivot).

[2026-07-25 /drain] TWO THINGS ABOUT THE ynab-mcp-new QUEUE BEFORE YOU RESOLVE THIS.

1. THERE IS A SYNTHETIC ROW IN THAT QUEUE. 'ynab-mcp-new-cbd — fresh probe issue' (owner: probe, no description, created 2026-07-25T14:00:14Z) is NOT real work. This is NOT a filesystem permission problem: .beads/embeddeddolt is drwx------ owned by sjaconette, and a shell write test on the directory succeeds. So it is bd/dolt-internal state.

Bearing on THIS issue's open question ('should that repo migrate to bd server mode, or should the embedded-mode export bug be fixed/reported upstream first?'): if the store is wedged read-only, then 'do not re-init a live queue' may be the wrong caution — the queue may already be unable to accept writes, which changes the cost of re-initializing from 'destroys live state' to 'recovers a stuck store'. title: workboard: --abandon for stale toolkit specs
description: The abandon-marker mechanism only covers Antigravity conversations; stale specs/<slug> dirs still require manual Status: deferred edits or deletion. Consider a symmetric one-command defer.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `python3 -m unittest discover -s .claude/skills/workboard -q` exits 0 with test count > 104 (baseline: 104 tests, all passing, verified now via `python3 -m unittest discover -s .claude/skills/workboard -q`).

2. `grep -c '"--defer"' .claude/skills/workboard/workboard.py` reports 1 (baseline now: 0) — a new `--defer` CLI flag exists, argparse-registered like `--abandon`.

3. `grep -c "^def defer_spec" .claude/skills/workboard/workboard.py` reports 1 (baseline now: 0) — a `defer_spec(repo, slug)` function exists that idempotently writes/updates a `Status: deferred` header line in `specs/<slug>/SPEC.md` (update in place if a `Status:` line already exists, insert one directly after the `# ` title line if absent), returning whether the spec was found.

4. `scan_toolkit_specs` captures a spec-level `Status: deferred` header the same way it already captures `Status: waiting` (currently only `"waiting"` is captured into `spec_rec["status"]` — verified: `sed -n '403,408p' .claude/skills/workboard/workboard.py` shows `if spec_status == "waiting": spec_rec["status"] = spec_status` with no `deferred` branch). After the fix, `grep -n 'spec_status == \"deferred\"\|spec_status in (\"waiting\", \"deferred\")\|spec_status in {\"waiting\", \"deferred\"}' .claude/skills/workboard/workboard.py` returns at least 1 match.

5. `attention_items` no longer emits a "stale"-state or "blocked"-state inbox item for a spec whose `SPEC.md` carries `Status: deferred` — a new unit test in `test_workboard.py` (e.g. `test_deferred_spec_is_excluded_from_stale_inbox` or equivalent name) constructs a spec with open tasks idle past `stale_days` and `Status: deferred`, asserts `attention_items(...)` returns no item for that spec, and passes. Verify post-fix with: `python3 -m unittest discover -s .claude/skills/workboard -q` (criterion 1 already covers the green-suite check; this item is the specific new test existing and being named descriptively per this repo's test-naming convention).

6. `reference.md`'s "One deliberate write exists" paragraph (currently: `sed -n '9,13p' .claude/skills/workboard/reference.md` shows it names only `--abandon <conv-id>` / `--abandon-stale`) is updated to also name `--defer <slug>`, and `SKILL.md`'s matching paragraph (currently: `sed -n '5,11p' .claude/skills/workboard/SKILL.md`, same "the explicit exceptions are..." sentence) is updated the same way — verified post-fix with `grep -c -- '--defer' .claude/skills/workboard/SKILL.md .claude/skills/workboard/reference.md`, each reporting ≥1.

Deferred/out of scope: `--defer-stale` (bulk variant mirroring `--abandon-stale`) is NOT required — the issue asks for "a symmetric one-command defer," and the singular `--defer <slug>` closes that gap; a bulk variant is a separate, smaller follow-up if wanted later. Also out of scope: changing `specs_open`/`tasks_open` top-level totals to exclude deferred specs — the issue's complaint is specifically about the needs-attention inbox (mirroring the Antigravity marker's inbox-suppression), not the summary counts.

4. `cd agent-console && ./scripts/check.sh` exits 0 and prints `check: PASS` (baseline: PASS, 219 tests). The worker must add at least one new unit test following the existing `test_adapts_repos_specs_sessions_and_inbox` pattern (test_parsers.py:231) that extends the `_assembled()` fixture with a `"spend": {"by_session": {"sid1": {"cost_microusd": N}}}` entry and asserts `board["repos"][0]["sessions"][0]` carries the matching cost value.
